nameStory: The 'Northern' part of this clam's name tells us where it lives - in the cooler waters of the North Atlantic. 'Dwarf' refers to its tiny size compared to other tellins, while 'tellin' comes from the Latin word for a type of thin, delicate seashell that was known to ancient Romans.
description: The Northern Dwarf-tellin is a tiny bivalve mollusk - essentially a miniature clam with two hinged shells. These delicate little shells are usually white to pale yellow and rarely grow longer than half an inch. Like other clams, the living animal has a soft body inside the protective shells and uses a muscular foot to burrow into sandy ocean bottoms. You're most likely to find their empty shells washed up on beaches rather than spotting the living clams themselves.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small - usually only 1/4 to 1/2 inch long, about the size of your pinky fingernail

idTips.label: Shape
idTips.description: Oval and flattened with a slightly pointed rear end, feeling thin and delicate when held

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Typically white, cream, or pale yellow with a smooth, glossy surface that catches light

idTips.label: Hinge
idTips.description: Two small cardinal teeth visible where the shells meet, feeling slightly rough to your fingertip

idTips.label: Interior
idTips.description: Inside surface is smooth and shiny white with a pearly luster

habitat: Found in sandy and muddy bottoms of shallow coastal waters from the low tide zone down to about 100 feet deep. Their empty shells wash up on sandy beaches throughout New England, especially after storms. Living clams prefer areas with good water circulation and soft sediments they can easily burrow into.

seasonality.spring: Fresh shells often wash ashore after spring storms and high tides. Look for them mixed in with other small shells and beach debris.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for beachcombing when shells are most visible on clean, wave-washed sand. Living clams are actively feeding in offshore sandy areas.
seasonality.fall: Storm-driven waves bring many shells to shore. Autumn beach walks often yield the best collections of small shells including tellins.
seasonality.winter: Shells continue washing up but may be buried under storm debris. Living clams burrow deeper into sediment during cold months.

funFact: Despite being only the size of a fingernail, these tiny clams can live for over 10 years and some individuals have been found buried more than 8 inches deep in sand - that's like a person digging themselves 40 feet underground!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with juvenile surf clams or other small bivalves on the beach. Remember the 'dwarf rule' - if it's smaller than a dime and oval-shaped with that telltale pointed rear end, you've likely found a dwarf-tellin rather than a baby of a larger clam species.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name 'Ameritella' literally means 'little American tellin,' reflecting both its small size and New World distribution. Many beachcombers overlook these tiny shells completely, focusing on larger, more obvious finds, but they're actually among the most abundant shells on our beaches.
compareHints: The Northern Dwarf-tellin is generally smaller and paler than its relative the Many-colored Tellin, which tends to have more pink, orange, or purple tinting. The Many-colored Tellin also has slightly more pronounced growth rings visible on its surface, while the Northern Dwarf-tellin appears smoother and more uniform in texture.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Many-colored Tellin differs from its close relative the Northern Dwarf-tellin by typically being slightly larger and showing more diverse coloration patterns.
